assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidities and the New Keynesian framework are the core of modern monetary-policy analysis. Staggered price and wage setting, interest-rate rules and the micro-founded policy framework shape how central banks reason and operate. The work combines foundational theory with lasting policy influence.
assessment.attribution: Calvo (time-dependent price setting) and Taylor (staggered contracts, and the policy rule) are the origin points. Woodford supplied the integrated micro-founded framework for monetary policy. Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets made major contributions to estimation and extension. A three-person limit forces hard exclusions, and the credit is arguably broader than any trio.
assessment.maturity: The contributions date from the late 1970s to the early 2000s and have decades of confirmation and use. Timing is not an obstacle.
uncertainties: Choosing three from a large group is contestable and could shift towards Gali or Gertler.
Gertler's overlap with the 2022 prize and with B002 may matter.
The framework's performance after 2008 and in the post-2021 inflation episode is debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work systematically brought electoral rules, constitutions, state capacity and fiscal policy into formal and empirical analysis. It created a coherent research programme in political economics with wide influence on public economics and development.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the central figures for the constitutional and electoral-rule programme. Besley's contributions on state capacity and political agency complement theirs. The trio is a natural and fairly clean grouping.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from the 1990s and 2000s and is well established and extensively built upon.
uncertainties: The 2024 prize for institutions and prosperity (Acemoglu, Johnson, Robinson) may reduce appetite for another political-economy award so soon.
Causal identification in the constitutional-effects work is open to challenge.
The broad scope makes the discovery description diffuse.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The alternating-offers bargaining model gave a tractable, foundational non-cooperative theory of negotiation. Its extension to decentralised markets links bargaining to search and market outcomes and is used across game theory, labour and monetary theory.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein (1982) is the clear originator. Wolinsky is credited through the Rubinstein–Wolinsky market-bargaining model. Binmore and others contributed to the strategic foundations, and the work builds on Ståhl's earlier model, which is not on the credited list. A sole or two-person award is plausible.
assessment.maturity: The work is more than 40 years old and fully confirmed as canonical.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would reward pure theory without direct empirical or policy application.
Whether Wolinsky's contribution is sufficient for co-recognition or Rubinstein should stand alone.
Credit for the Ståhl precursor is unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity transformed trade theory and empirics. It moved the unit of analysis from industries to firms, explained selection into exporting and gave a new channel for the gains from trade. It also reshaped quantitative trade work and the way data are used.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central contribution, with Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple on exporting versus FDI. Helpman has a long record of foundational trade-theory work. Redding contributed mainly to quantitative extensions, so he is better treated as a follower than a co-originator. Bernard and Jensen's empirical groundwork, and Eaton and Kortum's closely related work, are outside this list.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of confirmation and heavy use, and the framework is now textbook material.
uncertainties: Krugman's 2008 prize partly covers the new-trade-theory lineage.
Omitting empirical pioneers such as Bernard and Jensen is a weakness in the credit.
Overlap with the Helpman–Grossman candidate (B044).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Constructing long-run top-income and wealth series from tax data created a new empirical basis for inequality research and public debate. It has influenced public economics, tax policy and the measurement of distribution.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez are the clear originators of the top-income series, with Zucman extending the work to wealth and offshore holdings. Atkinson, who is deceased, was a key early contributor, and Piketty's later theoretical claims are more contested than the measurement work.
assessment.maturity: The top-income work dates from the early 2000s and has been widely replicated. The wealth and offshore-wealth extensions are newer and still debated.
uncertainties: Methodological disputes over the wealth estimates, and over r > g as a causal law.
Political salience may count for or against the award.
Overlap with B014 (Saez) and the ambiguity over whether Zucman should be included.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Models of fairness, reciprocity and inequity aversion explained systematic deviations from selfish-agent predictions in bargaining, public-goods and contract settings. They connect experimental evidence to tractable theory and have influenced contract and mechanism design.
assessment.attribution: The Fehr–Schmidt (1999) model and Fehr's experimental programme are central. Falk's contributions are significant but secondary. Rabin's 1993 reciprocity model is not on this list and is a major precursor, so the credit set is incomplete.
assessment.maturity: More than 25 years of citations and replication, and the work is thoroughly established, though its quantitative generality is debated.
uncertainties: Behavioural economics has been recognised several times (Kahneman, Thaler), which may reduce appetite.
External validity and the stability of the estimated social-preference parameters.
Incomplete precursor credit (Rabin and others).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Berry–Levinsohn–Pakes demand framework and the Ericson–Pakes dynamic industry model made it possible to estimate demand and market power with differentiated products. They underlie merger analysis, antitrust practice and modern empirical industrial organisation.
assessment.attribution: Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn are the authors of the core BLP estimator, with Pakes also central to dynamic models. Bresnahan and Reiss were important in the earlier structural-IO tradition, and the group is large, so the three-name limit forces a choice.
assessment.maturity: Developed in the 1990s, with 30 years of widespread use in academia and in practice.
uncertainties: Econometric and identification critiques of structural estimation.
Bresnahan's role as a possible rival to or substitute for one of the three.
Whether the committee prefers a methods-and-practice award in IO.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kiyotaki and Moore's credit-cycles model showed how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks. It is a cornerstone of macro-finance and was central to post-2008 analysis of financial frictions.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) is the clearest single contribution. Gertler and Gilchrist belong to the related financial-accelerator work, and Bernanke, Gertler and Gilchrist's accelerator is closely related. Gertler's overlap with the 2022 prize may reduce his case.
assessment.maturity: The work is nearly 30 years old and highly confirmed, with strong empirical and policy resonance after the financial crisis.
uncertainties: The 2022 prize to Bernanke, Diamond and Dybvig partly covers the financial-crisis theme.
Whether Kiyotaki–Moore or the Bernanke–Gertler–Gilchrist accelerator is seen as the primary contribution.
Competition from B001 for macro slots.
